text: After 10 hours with no social contact, people's brains reacted to pictures of other people the way a hungry brain reacts to food.
detail: In a brain-scan study of 40 adults, a midbrain area tied to craving lit up for social pictures after a day alone, much as it did for food pictures after a day without eating. Connection works like a need.

text: Your brain is still under construction through your teens and into your twenties, and the parts you use to understand other people are some of the last to finish.
detail: Researchers think the teen years may be a sensitive period: a window when what happens socially shapes the brain more than at other ages.

text: Young mice kept alone for two weeks grew thinner insulation on brain cells in the front of the brain. It did not recover when they went back to living with other mice.
detail: This is an animal study. The insulation, called myelin, helps brain signals travel fast. The same two weeks alone later in life did not do this, which points to a window when social contact matters most.

text: Being left out switches on some of the same brain areas as physical pain.
detail: In a small brain-scan study, people who were dropped from a simple ball-tossing game showed more activity in an area that also responds to the distress of physical pain.

text: Loneliness can follow you. Children and teens who felt lonely were more likely to have symptoms of depression months or even years later.
detail: A review of 63 studies with about 51,000 young people found this link up to nine years on. How long the loneliness lasted mattered more than how strong it felt.

text: Loneliness at school went up among teens in 36 of 37 countries between 2012 and 2018.
detail: This comes from surveys of about one million 15- and 16-year-olds around the world. If you feel it, you are far from the only one.

text: People aged 15 to 24 spend about 70% less time in person with friends than people that age did in 2003.
detail: The U.S. Surgeon General reported the drop: from about 150 minutes a day to about 40 minutes a day by 2020.

text: People with strong relationships were about 50% more likely to be alive at the end of long-term studies than people with weak ones.
detail: That is the combined result of 148 studies, mostly of adults, that followed people for about seven and a half years on average.

text: Wanting to be around friends more during your teen years is not a distraction from growing up. It is part of how the brain grows up.
detail: Researchers describe adolescence as a time of stronger need for contact with people your own age, and animal studies suggest that missing it during this period has effects it does not have at other ages.
